subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 16-year-old boy presents with rapid enlargement of a jaw mass. Biopsy shows sheets of lymphocytes with interspersed macrophages that impart a starry-sky appearance. Cytogenetic analysis is performed to confirm the diagnosis.
question: Which translocation is most likely to be identified?

options.text: t(14;18), placing BCL-2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter.
t(8;14), involving c-myc on chromosome 8 and the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus on chromosome 14.
t(11;14), involving cyclin D1 and the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus.
t(11;18), the characteristic abnormality of marginal zone lymphoma.
t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome seen in chronic myeloid leukemia.

explanation_correct: Burkitt lymphoma is defined by t(8;14), which translocates c-myc from chromosome 8 next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus on chromosome 14, driving constitutive c-myc expression and rapid proliferation. The patient's young age, jaw mass, and starry-sky histology with tingible body macrophages are classic. This is a mature B-cell neoplasm and is associated with EBV.

explanation_incorrect.A: t(14;18) involves BCL-2 and is characteristic of follicular lymphoma, which is indolent rather than rapidly growing.
explanation_incorrect.C: t(11;14) involving cyclin D1 and CD5 positivity defines mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive tumor of adult males.
explanation_incorrect.D: t(11;18) is associated with marginal zone MALT lymphoma arising in chronic inflammatory settings.
explanation_incorrect.E: t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukemia, not a mature B-cell lymphoma.

educationalObjective: Burkitt lymphoma is defined by t(8;14), placing c-myc under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 13-year-old child from central Africa presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw lesion and orbital involvement. Biopsy shows a starry-sky pattern of sheets of lymphocytes with tingible body macrophages. The tumor cells are positive for EBV.
question: Which form of Burkitt lymphoma does this presentation best illustrate?

options.text: The sporadic form, which typically involves the pelvis and abdomen.
The immunodeficiency-associated form, seen almost exclusively in patients with HIV.
Follicular lymphoma, which presents with painless waxing and waning lymphadenopathy.
The endemic (African) form, which classically involves the jaw and orbit.
Mantle cell lymphoma, which presents in adult males with late-stage disease.

explanation_correct: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma occurs in Africa, often in children, and classically presents with jaw and orbital lesions; it is strongly associated with EBV. The sporadic form, by contrast, more commonly involves the pelvis and abdomen. The starry-sky appearance reflects sheets of lymphocytes interspersed with tingible body macrophages. This patient's geography, age, and jaw lesion identify the endemic form.

explanation_incorrect.A: The sporadic form affects the pelvis and abdomen rather than the jaw and orbit and is less tightly linked to EBV.
explanation_incorrect.B: The immunodeficiency-associated form is tied to HIV and does not specifically produce the endemic jaw lesion pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent adult tumor with t(14;18) and painless waxing-and-waning nodes, not a starry-sky childhood tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mantle cell lymphoma occurs in adult males with t(11;14) and cyclin D1 expression, not in African children with jaw lesions.

educationalObjective: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma in Africa classically presents with jaw and orbital lesions and is EBV-associated, unlike the sporadic abdominal form.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 68-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging painless cervical node and B symptoms. Biopsy shows diffuse sheets of large B cells. Genetic studies show mutations in BCL-2 and BCL-6, and no t(14;18) or t(8;14) is detected.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Follicular lymphoma, an indolent tumor with a follicular growth pattern and t(14;18).
Burkitt lymphoma, a rapidly growing tumor with t(8;14) and a starry-sky pattern.
Mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive CD5-positive tumor with t(11;14).
Marginal zone lymphoma, an indolent tumor associated with chronic inflammation and t(11;18).
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults.

explanation_correct: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, though about 20% of cases occur in children. It is characterized by diffuse sheets of large B cells and mutations in BCL-2 and BCL-6. The absence of t(14;18) and t(8;14) and the diffuse large-cell morphology distinguish it from follicular and Burkitt lymphoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular lymphoma is indolent, has a follicular growth pattern and t(14;18), and lacks diffuse sheets of large cells.
explanation_incorrect.B: Burkitt lymphoma carries t(8;14), shows a starry-sky pattern, and affects adolescents and young adults rather than this older man.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5 positive with t(11;14) and cyclin D1 expression, which were not demonstrated here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Marginal zone lymphoma is linked to chronic inflammation and t(11;18) and is not composed of diffuse large B cells.

educationalObjective: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma and is associated with BCL-2 and BCL-6 mutations.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has had painless cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy for 2 years. The nodes alternately enlarge and shrink spontaneously. Biopsy shows a follicular growth pattern, and cytogenetics reveals t(14;18).
question: Which molecular abnormality explains the indolent behavior of this tumor?

options.text: t(14;18), which places BCL-2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter, increasing BCL-2 and inhibiting apoptosis.
t(8;14), which activates c-myc and drives rapid cellular proliferation.
t(11;14), which activates cyclin D1 and accelerates the G1-to-S transition.
Biallelic loss of p53, producing widespread genomic instability.
t(11;18), the characteristic translocation of marginal zone lymphoma.

explanation_correct: Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18), which moves BCL-2 from chromosome 18 next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus on chromosome 14. The resulting overexpression of BCL-2 inhibits apoptosis, allowing accumulation of neoplastic B cells. This underlies the indolent course and the classic painless waxing-and-waning lymphadenopathy. The follicular growth pattern on biopsy supports the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: t(8;14) activates c-myc and drives the rapid proliferation of Burkitt lymphoma, not the indolent follicular lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: t(11;14) activates cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive tumor rather than an indolent one.
explanation_incorrect.D: Loss of p53 causes genomic instability but is not the defining, indolence-producing lesion of follicular lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: t(11;18) is characteristic of marginal zone MALT lymphoma and does not explain this follicular tumor.

educationalObjective: Follicular lymphoma t(14;18) upregulates BCL-2, inhibiting apoptosis and producing an indolent waxing-and-waning course.
source: Generated from 10. Oncology.pdf - Pathology: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: mature B-cell neoplasms

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 64-year-old man presents with widespread lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone marrow involvement. Biopsy shows a monotonous population of small B cells. Immunophenotyping is CD5 positive and cyclin D1 positive, and cytogenetics show t(11;14).
question: Which of the following best characterizes this lymphoma?

options.text: Follicular lymphoma: indolent, CD5 negative, with t(14;18) and BCL-2 overexpression.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: CD5 positive but cyclin D1 negative and without t(11;14).
Mantle cell lymphoma: an aggressive tumor of adult males with t(11;14), cyclin D1 expression, CD5 positivity, and late-stage presentation.
Marginal zone lymphoma: associated with chronic inflammation and t(11;18).
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: an aggressive tumor with BCL-2 and BCL-6 mutations.

explanation_correct: Mantle cell lymphoma is a very aggressive mature B-cell neoplasm that occurs predominantly in adult males and typically presents with late-stage disease. It is defined by t(11;14), which places cyclin D1 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter, and the tumor cells express both cyclin D1 and CD5. The combination of CD5 positivity, cyclin D1 positivity, and t(11;14) is essentially diagnostic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular lymphoma is CD5 negative and carries t(14;18), not t(11;14), and follows an indolent course.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia can be CD5 positive but lacks cyclin D1 expression and t(11;14).
explanation_incorrect.D: Marginal zone lymphoma is linked to chronic inflammation and t(11;18) and does not express cyclin D1.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is defined by large cells and BCL-2/BCL-6 mutations rather than t(11;14) and cyclin D1.

educationalObjective: Mantle cell lymphoma is an aggressive CD5+/cyclin D1+ B-cell neoplasm with t(11;14) that typically presents at an advanced stage in older males.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing Sjogren syndrome and chronic atrophic gastritis develops a localized gastric mass. Biopsy shows a dense lymphoid infiltrate with reactive follicles. Testing for Helicobacter pylori is positive, and the patient is started on eradication therapy.
question: Which lymphoma is most likely, and what is a notable feature of its management?

options.text: Follicular lymphoma; it is treated with agents that reverse the t(14;18) translocation.
Mantle cell lymphoma; it is highly aggressive and requires immediate chemotherapy.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; it is unrelated to chronic antigenic stimulation.
Marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma; it is associated with chronic inflammation and may regress with H pylori eradication.
Burkitt lymphoma; it is EBV associated and typically occurs in children with jaw lesions.

explanation_correct: Marginal zone lymphoma arises in settings of chronic inflammation, such as Sjogren syndrome and chronic gastritis. Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by H pylori antigenic stimulation and carries t(11;18). A distinctive feature is that the tumor may regress when the inciting antigen is removed by eradicating H pylori. This makes it uniquely linked to an infectious trigger among the indolent B-cell lymphomas.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular lymphoma is associated with t(14;18) in adults but is not driven by H pylori and does not regress with antibiotic therapy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mantle cell lymphoma is aggressive with t(11;14) and cyclin D1 and is not linked to chronic H pylori gastritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is an aggressive large-cell tumor with BCL-2/BCL-6 mutations and is not the classic H pylori-associated MALT lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Burkitt lymphoma is an EBV-associated tumor of children with t(8;14), not an inflammation-driven adult gastric lymphoma.

educationalObjective: Marginal zone/MALT lymphoma arises in chronic inflammatory settings such as Sjogren syndrome and H pylori gastritis and can regress with antigen eradication.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 34-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40 per microliter presents with confusion, memory loss, and seizures. MRI shows a single ring-enhancing CNS lesion. His team considers two AIDS-defining conditions that can produce this appearance.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and the reason it must be distinguished from the alternative condition?

options.text: Cerebral toxoplasmosis; unlike lymphoma, it does not produce a ring-enhancing lesion on MRI.
Primary CNS lymphoma, an EBV-associated AIDS-defining malignancy whose ring-enhancing lesion must be distinguished from toxoplasmosis by CSF analysis or other studies.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, caused by JC virus and producing brightly enhancing mass lesions.
Systemic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which frequently produces a solitary ring-enhancing brain lesion in AIDS.
Burkitt lymphoma, an EBV-associated tumor that characteristically involves the CNS rather than the jaw or abdomen.

explanation_correct: Primary central nervous system lymphoma is an EBV-related malignancy and an AIDS-defining illness, occurring in severely immunocompromised patients. It produces variable neurologic symptoms and often a single ring-enhancing lesion on MRI. Because toxoplasmosis can produce a similar lesion in the same population, the two must be distinguished with CSF analysis or other laboratory studies. The distinction is critical because treatment differs fundamentally.

explanation_incorrect.A: Toxoplasmosis can also produce ring-enhancing lesions, so the absence of ring enhancement is not a valid way to exclude it.
explanation_incorrect.C: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy typically causes non-enhancing white matter lesions rather than a ring-enhancing mass.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is systemic and, although it can involve the CNS, it is not the classic AIDS-defining solitary ring-enhancing lesion described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Burkitt lymphoma is EBV associated but typically involves the jaw or abdomen in endemic and sporadic forms, not an isolated CNS mass.

educationalObjective: Primary CNS lymphoma is an EBV-associated AIDS-defining malignancy producing ring-enhancing lesions that must be distinguished from toxoplasmosis.
